formation.title: The Mu'minun Are Sovereign
formation.text:
From the cliff-walled madrasa at Tinmel, where Ibn Tumart preached that there is one God and one umma, your soldiers have descended to break the murabit veil and topple the Almoravids. Marrakesh has fallen; the green-and-white Almohad standards fly above the kasbahs of the Maghreb. From here, the question of what your Caliphate is to be can no longer be deferred.

Will you remain the Mahdi's avenging army, the Mu'minun who unite the umma by sword and sermon and brook no compromise? Or will you become a civilization in your own right, drawing the philosophers and scholars of al-Andalus into a court where Aristotle is read and Maimonides writes?

This choice unlocks a destiny path in the Traditions tab.

options.text: We are the army of the Mahdi: the umma will be one

modifiers.name: Mahdist Revolution
modifiers.text: Ibn Tumart's puritanical reform burns through the Caliphate. The Mu'minun bear arms with the certainty of the saved, and heretics know no quarter; but the watchful inquisitors of the Almohad creed leave little room for the older schools and their tolerated minorities.

options.text: Marrakesh shall be the new Cordoba: a court of philosophers

modifiers.name: Caliphal Civilization
modifiers.text: Yaqub al-Mansur's Marrakesh becomes a beacon of falsafa: Ibn Rushd commenting on Aristotle, Maimonides composing the Mishneh Torah at his court, paper mills humming and Andalusi scholars filling the libraries. The Caliphate rests easy in its grandeur, perhaps too easy.

advances.name: The Tinmel Foundation
advances.text: Ibn Tumart's mountain madrasa at Tinmel, in the Sus valley of the High Atlas, was the cradle of the Almohad movement. Here he proclaimed the Mahdiyya, taught the doctrine of divine unity (tawhid), and gathered the Masmuda tribes that would become the army of Abd al-Mu'min.

event.title: The Mosque at Tinmel
event.text: High in the Sus valley, on the saddle where Ibn Tumart first gathered the Masmuda tribes and proclaimed the Mahdiyya, Abd al-Mu'min has commissioned the great mosque of Tinmel. Its walls shelter the founder's tomb. The pilgrims who come to it are no ordinary worshippers: they are the recruits of an unfinished movement, and they ask whether the revolutionary moment is to be sustained or settled. The Council of Fifty awaits the Caliph's word.

options.text: Sustain the revolution: the sword has not yet finished

modifiers.name: Zeal of Tinmel
modifiers.text: The Mahdi's followers march down from the Atlas with the fervor of revelation. New recruits flock to the cause, drilled by the Mu'minun in the harsh discipline of the Almohad creed.

options.text: Consolidate the movement: the foundations must be set

modifiers.name: Consolidation of the Movement
modifiers.text: Rather than press the moment, the Caliph sinks roots: the council of fifty is formalized, the Berber tribes given their ranks, and the new orthodoxy quietly entrenched in administration.

advances.name: Masmuda Infantry
advances.text: Unlike the Almoravids who drew on Saharan camel cavalry, the Almohad army was built around the dense infantry formations of the semi-nomadic Masmuda Berbers of the High Atlas: spearmen and javelin throwers organized by tribal hierarchy.

advances.name: Zenata Horsemen
advances.text: The Zenata Berbers of the high plateau provided the light cavalry of the Maghrebi armies: skirmishers and lancers who fought with the karr wa farr tactic of attack and feigned retreat, mounted on the swift North African horse.

advances.name: Kasbah Tradition
advances.text: Almohad governors ruled their cities from the kasbah, a fortified citadel rising above the medina with its own walls, gates, granaries, and barracks. Marrakesh, Fez, Sevilla and Rabat all received Almohad kasbahs.

advances.name: Council of Ten
advances.text: The Almohad state was governed by a hierarchy of councils descending from the Caliph: the Ahl al-dar (Council of Ten) of close kinsmen and trusted shaykhs, then the Council of Fifty, and below it the assemblies of the Masmuda tribes. This stratified council government bound the regime tightly to its Berber base.

advances.name: Almohad Minaret Tradition
advances.text: The square sandstone minaret of the Koutoubia in Marrakesh, copied at the Hassan Tower in Rabat and the Giralda in Sevilla, became the signature of Almohad religious architecture: monumental, austere, and visible across half the kingdom.

advances.name: Falsafa
advances.text: The Almohad Caliphs, Abu Yaqub Yusuf and Yaqub al-Mansur in particular, gathered around themselves the philosophers of al-Andalus: Ibn Tufayl, Ibn Rushd (Averroes), and the Jewish thinker Maimonides. Their Marrakesh court became the high point of medieval Aristotelian commentary.

event.title: Ibn Rushd of Cordoba
event.text: Abu al-Walid Muhammad ibn Rushd, qadi of Cordoba and physician to the Caliph, has completed his Long Commentary on Aristotle's Metaphysics. In Cairo and Toledo and Paris, his name is spoken with awe. At your court, the Jewish philosopher Maimonides has just completed the Guide for the Perplexed. The fuqaha of Marrakesh are not pleased: they speak of the philosophers as foreign infiltrators, and demand a return to the pure creed of Ibn Tumart.

options.text: Defend the philosophers: the Caliphate must lead in thought

modifiers.name: Court of the Commentator
modifiers.text: Ibn Rushd's commentaries are read in the very court of the Caliph; Jewish, Christian, and Muslim philosophers speak as equals on metaphysics. Marrakesh becomes the lighthouse of falsafa, drawing scholars from Toledo to Baghdad.

options.text: Burn the books: orthodoxy must not be diluted

modifiers.name: The Orthodoxy Triumphant
modifiers.text: Ibn Rushd is exiled, his books burned in the souk of Cordoba. The Caliphate's preachers march behind purified doctrine; the conversion of subject peoples accelerates, the unity of the umma reaffirmed.

advances.name: Andalusi Crossbowmen
advances.text: The cities of al-Andalus furnished the Caliphate with its missile infantry: townsmen trained on the foot crossbow, descendants of the Cordoban tradition, who supplemented the Berber spear with the steel-tipped bolt.

advances.name: Caravan Economy
advances.text: Sijilmasa and Wadan stood at the desert end of the trans-Saharan trade. Almohad governors built funduqs in the cities, organized caravan routes, and taxed the gold-and-salt traffic that bound the Sahel to the Mediterranean.

advances.name: Maliki Revival
advances.text: Although Ibn Tumart and the early Caliphs persecuted the Maliki fuqaha and burned copies of the Muwatta, by the reign of al-Mansur the older school had quietly reasserted itself. The fiqh of the qadis returned to Maliki precedent, anchoring the regime in the inherited jurisprudence of the Maghreb.

advances.name: Jihad in al-Andalus
advances.text: Each Caliph in turn crossed the strait at the head of a great army to wage jihad against the Christian kingdoms: at Alarcos in 1195, Yaqub al-Mansur shattered Castile, and the green-and-white standards reached as far as Toledo. The Almohad campaigns set the model for the long Iberian war.

effects.name: Damage Done versus Heathens in Battle

event.title: Las Navas de Tolosa
event.text: On the high meseta of Tolosa, the combined hosts of Castile, Aragon, and Navarre have broken the Caliphal army. Caliph al-Nasir flees south through the Sierra Morena; the camp tents and the green standards lie scattered. The very nucleus of Andalusi defense is hollowed. From Marrakesh, the question is sharp: do we cross the strait again with everything we have, or do we retrench in Africa and let al-Andalus fend for itself?

options.text: Cross again: every man and every sword to Iberia

modifiers.name: Andalusi Legions
modifiers.text: Stung by defeat at the great battle, the Caliph calls every able man across the strait. Fresh Andalusi infantry and Berber jund pour into the Iberian field once more, the morale of the realm forged anew in vengeance.

options.text: Withdraw south: the African heart will not be lost

modifiers.name: African Bastion
modifiers.text: The Caliph withdraws to Marrakesh and refortifies the Maghreb. If al-Andalus must be lost, then at least the African heart will hold; revenues recover and garrisons swell.

advances.name: Christian Mercenary Brigades
advances.text: By the late twelfth century the Almohads, like the Andalusi taifa kings before them, had begun to recruit Iberian Christian mercenaries by the thousand: Castilian knights serving in the Caliph's guard, Norman foot soldiers garrisoning provincial towns, paid in silver and given houses in Marrakesh.

advances.name: Ribat Tradition
advances.text: The ribat was a fortified frontier monastery where lay volunteers performed military service alongside their devotions. Strung along the coast from Sale to Sus to Sfax, the ribats trained the murabitun: pious frontiersmen who answered the Caliph's call.

advances.name: Marrakeshi Metalwork
advances.text: The forges of the Almohad capital armed both the Berber jund and the Andalusi infantry, with Damascene-style steel from Iberian iron and brass-fitted scimitars copied from the eastern lands. The Caliphal armouries set the standard for the western Mediterranean.

advances.name: Maghrebi Astronomy
advances.text: The Andalusi astronomers Ibn Tufayl, al-Bitruji, and Jabir ibn Aflah worked at the Almohad court, refining the Ptolemaic system, building observatories, and producing the astronomical tables that would later feed Toledo and Paris.

advances.name: The Monumental Caliphate
advances.text: Yaqub al-Mansur made monumental architecture an instrument of legitimacy. Ribat al-Fath, the Hassan Tower, the great mosque at Sevilla with its Giralda, the Koutoubia in Marrakesh: across the Caliphate, the Almohad name was raised in stone, austere and immense.

event.title: The Hassan Tower
event.text: On the bluff above the Bou Regreg, where Abd al-Mu'min once raised a kasbah, Caliph Yaqub al-Mansur has commanded a vast new capital: Ribat al-Fath, the Fortress of Victory. Its centerpiece is to be a mosque larger than any in the western lands, with a minaret to dwarf the Koutoubia. The masons quarry sandstone by the thousand and the imperial treasury bleeds. Some courtiers urge moderation: better to finish the Koutoubia and adorn the cities we have, than to build a new metropolis we may not need.

options.text: Build Ribat al-Fath: the Caliphate deserves a capital of conquest

modifiers.name: Ribat al-Fath
modifiers.text: Yaqub al-Mansur founds his vast new capital at the mouth of the Bou Regreg: a fortified city of conquest, with the Hassan Tower rising above it. Construction crews work with imperial speed across the realm.

options.text: Adorn the existing cities: glory belongs to Marrakesh

modifiers.name: Glory of Marrakesh
modifiers.text: Rather than build anew, the Caliph adorns the existing capital. The Koutoubia is finished in jewel-like elegance, the gates of the city rebuilt, and the Almohad name carries weight from Sevilla to Cairo.

advances.name: Andalusi Silk Weaving
advances.text: From Almeria to Granada, the silk workshops of al-Andalus, inheritors of the Cordoban tradition, wove the finest textiles in the western Mediterranean. The Caliph's tiraz workshops produced the embroidered robes of state worn from Marrakesh to Cairo.

advances.name: Sufi Brotherhoods
advances.text: Spreading from the zawiyas of the Maghreb, popular Sufi orders, the Shadhili and Qadiri among them, took root in city and village alike. Their saints (awliya) and spiritual genealogies bound peripheral peoples to the urban Islamic culture and assimilated newcomers to the Caliphal orthodoxy.

advances.name: Caliphal Arsenals
advances.text: Imperial arsenals at Marrakesh, Fez, and Sevilla supplied the Caliph's standing forces: jund cavalry, Andalusi infantry, and the imperial bodyguard. Centralized armament made it possible to field the largest armies in the western Islamic world.

advances.name: Trans-Saharan Gold
advances.text: The gold of the Wadi Sus and the salt of Taghaza moved through Almohad customs houses on its way to Mediterranean markets. The Caliphate's tax revenues swelled in proportion to the trans-Saharan flow.

advances.name: Sharifian Legitimacy
advances.text: The descendants of the Almohad Caliphs and the later Maghrebi dynasties claimed sharifian descent from the Prophet, lending their rule a legitimacy independent of the Abbasid caliphate or any external authority.

advances.name: Maghrebi Corsairs
advances.text: From Sale to Tetouan to Algiers, the corsair ports of the Maghreb sent fast xebecs and galleots into the western Mediterranean and the Atlantic, raiding European shipping and bringing slaves and silver back to the Caliphate.

advances.name: Kharaj Reform
advances.text: Reformed land taxation distinguished kharaj on conquered estates from ushr tithes on Muslim freeholds, regularizing the fiscal foundation of the Caliphate and stabilizing revenue across rural areas.

advances.name: The Mahalla
advances.text: The Caliph governed from a mobile encampment, the mahalla, that moved between Marrakesh, Fez, and the provinces. This itinerant rulership kept rebellious tribes in check and reasserted central authority by direct presence.

advances.name: Caliphal Modernization
advances.text: Following the example of the Ottoman nizam-i-cedid and the Egyptian reforms of Muhammad Ali, the Caliphate's officers drilled regular infantry in European fashion, importing instructors and modern muskets to face the new age of warfare.

advances.name: Anti-Colonial Resistance
advances.text: Where Algiers fell and Tunis became a protectorate, the Caliphate stood against European encroachment: diplomatic plays in the European courts, supply of irregular forces in the hinterland, and the doctrine that the Maghreb was not for sale.

advances.name: Industrial Revival
advances.text: Modern arsenals at Casablanca, shipyards at Sale, and printed schoolbooks in Fez signal the Caliphate's late embrace of industrial technique, an attempt to meet European powers as a peer rather than as a subject.

advances.name: Maghrebi Printing Press
advances.text: Late but determined, Arabic printing presses at Fez and Marrakesh produce schoolbooks, gazettes, and translated European works. Print culture penetrates the urban literate classes and reshapes the public sphere.

destiny.name: Destiny of the Caliphate
destiny.text: The choice made at Marrakesh sets the long course of the realm. Whether by the sword of Tinmel or the libraries of al-Andalus, the Almohad project must now be carried to its conclusion.

conditions.text: Stability at least 25

event.title: The Long Course
event.text: The choice made on the day of formation has rippled out through the realm. Couriers ride south to the Sus, north to the strait, east to Tunis: the Caliphate has settled on its path, and the next generation of viziers will know what is asked of them. The destiny of the Almohad Caliphate is taking shape.

options.text: May our cause prosper

destiny.name: Cross the Strait
destiny.text: The Mahdist host crosses the Strait of Gibraltar in force. The first prizes are the Levante and the central Meseta: Valencia and Toledo. Every soldier sent across the strait is one more sword for the umma.

event.title: The Sword Crosses the Strait
event.text: The Mahdist army has crossed the Strait of Gibraltar in force, and the Levante and the central Meseta lie in your hand. Valencia is taken; the gates of Toledo open to the green-and-white standards. The Christian kingdoms reel from the shock. The Caliph's preachers ride ahead of the army, declaring the restoration of Islam to the lands the Visigoths once stole.

options.text: Onward: the umma is restored

destiny.name: The Western March
destiny.text: The Atlantic shore beckons. Push the green-and-white standards through Coimbra to the mouth of the Tagus, taking Lisbon and the Portuguese coast for the Caliphate.

conditions.text: Own Lisbon, or a subject owns it
Own Coimbra, or a subject owns it
Army size at least 50
Prestige at least 50

event.title: The Atlantic Shore
event.text: Coimbra has fallen and Lisbon kneels beneath the Hassan Tower's lesser cousins. The Atlantic shore is yours from the Sus to the Douro. Now the question is how to hold what has been won: by raiding column and continuous campaign, hardening the army for the next push? Or by settling the new lands with Berber colonists and Andalusi qadis, to root the conquest in stable government?

options.text: March on: the campaign must not slacken

modifiers.name: Atlantic Jihad
modifiers.text: The army is kept on continuous campaign along the Atlantic shore. Loot is plentiful, supply trains run thick, and reinforcements move easily; but the constant war-spending stokes inflation in the cities.

options.text: Settle the conquest: bring the qadis and the colonists

modifiers.name: Settlement of the Levante
modifiers.text: Berber colonists and Andalusi qadis are settled across the conquered lands. Cultures are integrated, separatism falls, and the realm becomes durably plural.

destiny.name: Reconquista Reversed
destiny.text: From Pamplona to Barcelona by way of Zaragoza, the last Christian kingdoms of Iberia are broken or absorbed, and Seville, where the Almohads raised their great minaret, is rebuilt to twice its size as the Caliph's seat in al-Andalus. The umma is restored to Visigothic Spain. Ribat al-Fath rules from sea to sea.

event.title: The Caliphate Restored
event.text: From Pamplona to Barcelona, the last crowned Christian heads have submitted, fled, or fallen. The Visigothic kingdom is undone; the Caliphate stretches from the Pyrenees to the Niger. Now the courtiers debate the meaning of the moment: is the Caliph the universal hammer of unbelief, who will press on into the Pyrenees and beyond? Or has the natural frontier been reached, and is it time to fortify the line and consolidate?

options.text: We are the universal Caliphate of the West

modifiers.name: Caliphate of the West
modifiers.text: The Caliph claims universal authority over the western umma. New casus belli ripen quickly, war scores tilt favorably, and peace negotiations bend to imperial will. But the realm's people grow weary of endless campaign.

options.text: The Pyrenees are the frontier; we hold the line

modifiers.name: The Pyrenean Frontier
modifiers.text: The Pyrenees become the limes of the Caliphate. Auxiliaries hold the passes, the muster rolls grow fat, and the religious state hardens; the Caliph does not pick fights beyond the natural frontier.

destiny.name: The Salt Road
destiny.text: South of the Sahara, the salt-and-gold caravans wait at the desert wells of Wadan and Walata. Plant the Caliph's banner over the Adrar oases, and the trans-Saharan trade flows into Marrakesh's coffers.

conditions.text: Path of the Caliphal court chosen
Own Wadan, or a subject owns it
Own Walata, or a subject owns it
Gold at least 1000

event.title: Wells of Wadan
event.text: The wells of Wadan and Walata are now in Almohad hands. The salt slabs of Taghaza, the gold dust of the Wadi Sus, the date harvests of the Adrar: all flow upward to Marrakesh. The desert routes have a master, and the Caliph's customs houses bleed silver out of every passing caravan.

options.text: Marrakesh enriches itself by the desert

destiny.name: Bilad al-Sudan
destiny.text: Beyond the desert lies the Land of the Blacks: Timbuktu of the libraries, Djenne of the mud-brick mosque. With caravan stops in three places along the desert road and a treasury that the world envies, the Caliphate joins the river-cities to the Maghreb.

conditions.text: Own Timbuktu, or a subject owns it
Own Djenné, or a subject owns it
Owns a location with
Gold at least 2000

event.title: The River of Black Gold
event.text: Timbuktu and Djenne, the river-cities of the Niger, have come into the Caliphate's orbit. Their scholars copy Maliki fiqh from Andalusi exemplars; their gold dust flows up the salt route to Sijilmasa. The question of how to govern this new realm divides the diwan: rule lightly through native emirs, leveraging local prestige? Or pull the trade down to Marrakesh, and let the bankers of the capital take the profit?

options.text: Govern through native emirs: the Caliph as suzerain

modifiers.name: Sudani Emirates
modifiers.text: Native emirs rule the Sahel under Caliphal suzerainty. Subjects are loyal, diplomatic ties multiply, and goodwill propagates from the Niger to the Atlas.

options.text: Centralize the trade: Marrakesh is the bank of the Sahel

modifiers.name: Bankers of Marrakesh
modifiers.text: The capital becomes the great clearing house of the western trade. Merchants are subsidized, building costs eased by abundant credit, and inflation tamed; but the diplomatic corps is starved as merchants run the embassies.

destiny.name: The Two Shores
destiny.text: Niani submits, gold flows up through the capital market, and the Caliphate stands as the great economic power between the Mediterranean and the Niger. Marrakesh, grown to twice its size, is the new Cordoba and the new Cairo at once.

event.title: The Caliphate of Two Shores
event.text: Niani has submitted, gold flows through the capital market, and the Caliphate is a junction of trans-Saharan and Mediterranean wealth without equal. The diwan debates the next great project: shall the realm turn outward to the sea, building fleets to project Almohad power across the Mediterranean? Or shall Marrakesh become the new Cordoba in earnest, a cosmopolis of Andalusi philosophy and Sudani scholarship?

options.text: Build the imperial fleet: command the western sea

modifiers.name: The Imperial Marketplace
modifiers.text: Almohad fleets command the western Mediterranean. Sea trade flourishes, sailors flock to the corsair ports, and naval traditions deepen by the season.

options.text: Make Marrakesh the cosmopolis of two continents

modifiers.name: The Andalusi Cosmopolis
modifiers.text: Marrakesh becomes the new Cordoba: scholars from Tlemcen and Timbuktu, philosophers from Granada and Fez, recover the realm from the marks of war and weave a quiet web of agents across the Mediterranean. But the Caliphate looks inward, not outward to the open sea.

units.name: Masmuda Spearmen
units.text: Heavy infantry levied from the semi-nomadic Berbers of the High Atlas, organized by tribal hierarchy and fighting in dense formations.

units.name: Zenata Lancers
units.text: Light cavalry of the Maghrebi plateau, masters of the karr wa farr tactic of charge and feigned retreat.

units.name: Andalusi Crossbowmen
units.text: Urban militia of al-Andalus trained on the foot crossbow, providing the Caliphate's missile infantry alongside the Berber spear.

units.name: Christian Mercenary Militia
units.text: Iberian Christian mercenaries hired in regiments by the late Caliphate, paid in silver and quartered in Marrakesh: Castilian knights, Norman footmen, and adventurers from the Pyrenees.

units.name: Corsair Xebec
units.text: A swift Maghrebi galley with combined oar and lateen-rigged sail, raiding European shipping from Sale to Algiers and threading the Strait of Gibraltar.

buildings.name: Almohad Kasbah
buildings.text: A fortified citadel built atop the city, with its own walls, granary, barracks, and the governor's palace. The Almohad kasbah projects imperial authority into every Maghrebi city.

buildings.name: Almohad Minaret
buildings.text: A vast square minaret in the Almohad style, of dressed sandstone with sebka panels and arched balcony: the model for the Koutoubia, Hassan Tower, and Giralda.

buildings.name: House of Wisdom
buildings.text: A scholarly institution combining madrasa, library, and translation bureau. Andalusi philosophers, Jewish physicians, and Maghrebi astronomers all serve under the Caliph's patronage.

buildings.name: Funduq Quarter
buildings.text: An urban district of caravanserais, warehouses, and merchant houses where trans-Saharan caravans terminate and Mediterranean shipping is unloaded. The funduq is the engine of Maghrebi urban wealth.

buildings.name: Coastal Ribat
buildings.text: A fortified frontier monastery on the coast, where lay volunteers do military service alongside their devotions. The ribats line the Atlantic and Mediterranean shores from Sale to Sfax.

buildings.name: Caliphal Armoury
buildings.text: An imperial arms workshop producing weaponry for the jund and the Andalusi infantry, equipped with forges, foundries, and the corps of armourers attached to the Caliph's standing forces.

buildings.name: Andalusi Silk Workshop
buildings.text: A tiraz workshop in the al-Andalus tradition, weaving the finest brocade and embroidered robes of state, exported from Almeria and Granada to all the courts of the Mediterranean.

buildings.name: Caliphal Academy
buildings.text: A modern military and scientific academy on the Ottoman nizam-i-cedid model, teaching artillery, fortification, geometry, and modern languages to a new generation of officers and bureaucrats.

buildings.name: Mustering Ribat
buildings.text: A walled camp with barracks, a parade ground and a pay office, where the Caliph's standing army gathers and is counted and paid before it marches. Its model is Ribat al-Fath, the camp Abd al-Mu'min founded in 1150 at the mouth of the Bou Regreg for the armies crossing to al-Andalus. The city of Rabat grew out of it.

buildings.name: Council of Jihad
buildings.text: An imperial council of war and warden, fortified within the kasbah, where standing legions are mustered, frontier garrisons paid, and the unending campaigns of the western umma directed.

buildings.name: Caliphal Treasury
buildings.text: The imperial mint and bullion vault of Marrakesh, where Sudani gold is struck into dinars, fine silks brocaded with the Caliph's name leave for foreign courts, and the bankers of two continents render their accounts.

list.name: Talaba
list.text: The Almohad cadre of theological-administrative students, schooled in Ibn Tumart's tawhid doctrine at the great madrasa of the Kutubiyya and the lodge at Tinmel. Drawn first from the Masmuda chiefs of the High Atlas and later from the wider empire, the talaba supplied the qadis, governors, and tax assessors of the early Caliphate. They displaced the inherited Maliki ulama as the institutional clergy of the realm, training a literate class loyal to the Mu'minid dynasty rather than to the long-rooted Andalusi-Maghrebi fuqaha whose authority the Almohads had come to reform.

conditions.text: Sunnism religion

list.name: Ahl al-Jama'a
list.text: The Almohad inner council, descended from Ibn Tumart's original Council of Ten and the broader Council of Fifty. It comprised the chiefs of the Masmuda confederation (Hintata, Tinmel, Ganfisa, Hargha) alongside the dynastic Mu'minid kin. The jama'a confirmed succession, apportioned campaign commands, and held formal precedence over civil administrators. It made the Almohad state a tribal-aristocratic confederation in caliphal dress, with all the vigor and the brittleness that implied: the same chiefs whose levies broke the Castilians at Alarcos in 1195 abandoned the realm into civil war after Las Navas in 1212.

list.name: Office of the 'Alama
list.text: Every decree from Marrakesh carried the 'alama: a short phrase of praise to God set at its head in thick letters, in the Caliph's own hand or that of the one secretary trusted with it. A letter without it was only paper. The chancery wrote in rhymed prose and sent its letters to every province: the appointment of a governor, news of a victory, a ruling on doctrine. Some three hundred survive. Under secretaries like Abu Ja'far ibn 'Atiyya these letters bound the Maghreb and al-Andalus into one administration. The Hafsids, Marinids and Nasrids kept the 'alama after the Almohads were gone.

conditions.text: Owns Marrakesh

list.name: Sikka Almohad
list.text: The imperial mint of Marrakesh, whose square-flan gold dinar (the dobla almohade) and silver dirham became the most trusted coinage of the western Mediterranean. The Christian crowns of Iberia minted millares in conscious imitation, and Almohad gold circulated as far as the fairs of Champagne. The mint's prestige rested on its purity, near 98% gold, and the Caliph's strict control of the assay; loosen that grip, and the coin debased itself into the inflation of the late Mu'minids.
